title: Grade 8 Science — Wed, May 28
description: Microorganisms — Day 3 of 5: Harmful microorganisms — diseases, food spoilage, food preservation
subject: science

questions.question: Pathogens are microorganisms that:
questions.explanation: Pathogens = disease-causing microorganisms. Examples: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (TB), Vibrio cholerae (cholera), Plasmodium (malaria), Influenza virus (flu). Not all microorganisms are pathogens.

questions.question: Match the disease to its causative agent: Tuberculosis / Cholera / Common cold / Malaria
questions.explanation: TB = Mycobacterium tuberculosis (bacteria). Cholera = Vibrio cholerae (bacteria). Common cold = Rhinovirus (virus). Malaria = Plasmodium falciparum (protozoa). Learn these key pathogens!

questions.question: Diseases that spread from one person to another are called:
questions.explanation: Communicable diseases spread via air, water, food, contact, or vectors. Examples: cold, TB, cholera, malaria. Non-communicable: heart disease, diabetes (not spread by microorganisms).

questions.question: Vectors in disease transmission are:
options: Organisms (like mosquitoes) that carry and transmit pathogens from one host to another
The medicine used to treat disease
questions.explanation: Vectors carry pathogens without causing disease in themselves. Mosquito (Anopheles) → malaria (Plasmodium). Mosquito (Aedes aegypti) → dengue fever. Housefly → typhoid, cholera (mechanically).

questions.question: Food spoilage by microorganisms occurs because they:
options: Produce enzymes and toxins that decompose food, changing colour, smell, and taste
questions.explanation: Spoilage microorganisms produce enzymes that break down food proteins, fats, carbohydrates. They also produce toxins. Signs of spoilage: bad smell, discolouration, sliminess, mould growth.

questions.question: Pasteurisation (used for milk) involves:
options: Heating milk to 70–72°C for 15–20 seconds, then rapidly cooling it
Adding chemicals to milk to kill bacteria
Filtering milk through very fine membranes
questions.explanation: Pasteurisation: heat to 70-72°C (enough to kill pathogens) then rapid cooling to prevent regrowth. Named after Louis Pasteur. Kills harmful bacteria without destroying nutrients or taste significantly.

questions.question: Why does salting preserve food (like pickles, fish)?
options: Salt draws out moisture (osmosis), creating a hostile environment where microorganisms cannot survive
Salt changes the pH to neutral which stops microorganisms
questions.explanation: High salt concentration → osmosis draws water OUT of bacterial cells → bacteria shrink (plasmolysis) and die/cannot grow. Same principle for sugar preservation (jams, jellies).

questions.question: Refrigeration preserves food by:
options: Slowing down microbial growth and enzyme activity (doesn't kill but inhibits)
questions.explanation: Cold temperatures slow enzyme reactions and microbial metabolism — slows (doesn't stop) growth. Freezing can stop growth entirely. Some bacteria (psychrophiles) still grow in refrigerators! Always check expiry dates.

questions.question: Food poisoning caused by Staphylococcus aureus is dangerous because:
options: The bacteria multiply in the gut and spread to blood
The bacteria produce toxins IN the food BEFORE eating — toxins remain even if bacteria are killed by cooking
The bacteria are resistant to stomach acid
The bacteria produce viruses inside the body
questions.explanation: S. aureus produces heat-stable toxins in food. Even if the bacteria are killed by cooking, the toxins survive! This is why proper food storage (refrigeration, preventing contamination) is critical.

questions.question: Which method of food preservation uses high-energy radiation to kill microorganisms?
questions.explanation: Food irradiation uses gamma rays, X-rays, or electron beams to kill bacteria, moulds, and insects. Used for spices, fruits, meat. Food does NOT become radioactive. Approved by WHO.

questions.question: Why should antibiotics NOT be overused or misused?
options: Antibiotics are too expensive to waste
Overuse kills all gut bacteria permanently
Overuse leads to antibiotic-resistant bacteria ('superbugs') that no longer respond to treatment
Antibiotics cause immediate allergic reactions in everyone
questions.explanation: Antibiotic resistance: bacteria mutate and survive antibiotic exposure. Resistant strains spread. MRSA, MDR-TB are examples. WHO warns this is a global health crisis. Always complete the full course of antibiotics.

questions.question: The disease caused by Clostridium tetani enters the body through:
options: Deep puncture wounds (nail, bite) where anaerobic conditions allow bacteria to grow
questions.explanation: Clostridium tetani (tetanus) lives in soil. Enters via deep wounds — thrives in anaerobic (low-oxygen) conditions. Produces neurotoxin causing muscle spasms ('lockjaw'). Prevented by DPT vaccine.

questions.question: Aflatoxins (produced by Aspergillus fungi on stored grain) are dangerous because they are:
options: Potent carcinogens (cancer-causing agents) that can cause liver cancer
questions.explanation: Aspergillus mould grows on improperly stored grains, peanuts. Produces aflatoxins — among the most potent naturally occurring carcinogens. Proper grain storage (dry, cool) prevents aflatoxin contamination.

questions.question: Personal hygiene practices that prevent microbial infections include:
options: Washing hands with soap, drinking safe water, covering cuts, not sharing personal items, cooking food thoroughly
Avoiding all contact with other people
questions.explanation: Hygiene breaks the chain of infection: handwashing (removes pathogens), clean water (prevents waterborne diseases), food safety (kills foodborne pathogens), wound care (prevents entry). Soap kills bacteria by disrupting cell membranes.

questions.question: Which diseases can be prevented by vaccination?
options: All bacterial, viral, fungal, and protozoan diseases
Polio, measles, tetanus, hepatitis B, influenza (diseases with available vaccines)
questions.explanation: Vaccines exist for specific diseases: polio (Salk/Sabin), measles (MMR), DPT (diphtheria/pertussis/tetanus), hepatitis B, influenza, COVID-19. Not all diseases have vaccines yet (e.g., malaria vaccine only recently developed).
